# Introduction

This report uses the UCI Heart Disease dataset (Janosi et al., 1989), which contains clinical data on 920 patients who were evaluated for coronary heart disease at four sites: the Cleveland Clinic Foundation (n = 303), the Hungarian Institute of Cardiology in Budapest (n = 294), University Hospitals in Zurich and Basel, Switzerland (n = 123), and the Long Beach VA Medical Center (n = 200). 

The dataset includes 13 potential predictors, including demographic characteristics (age, sex) and cardiovascular measures such as chest pain type, resting blood pressure, serum cholesterol, and maximum heart rate achieved during exercise testing. The outcome is an angiographic diagnosis of coronary heart disease, originally scored from 0 (no disease) to 4. In this report, the outcome is categorized as disease present (scores 1-4) or absent (score 0).

The objectives of this analysis are to:

1. Describe the demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population,
   overall and by heart disease status.
2. Compare the prevalence of heart disease across the four study sites.

# Data

```{r load-data}
# cleaned by code/01_clean_data.R
heart <- readRDS(here::here("output", "heart_clean.rds"))
```

The dataset contains `r nrow(heart)` patients at four clinical sites.

# Patient Characteristics

```{r table1}
# created by code/02_make_table1.R
readRDS(here::here("output", "table1.rds"))
```

```{r table1-stats}
by_disease <- heart |>
  group_by(disease) |>
  summarise(
    male = mean(sex == 1),
    asym = mean(cp == 4),
    hr = median(thalach, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

yes <- filter(by_disease, disease == "Yes")
no <- filter(by_disease, disease == "No")
```

Table 1 summarizes the demographic and clinical characteristics of the
`r nrow(heart)` patients, overall and by heart disease status. Continuous variables
are presented as median (IQR) and categorical variables as n (%), and p-values
compare patients with and without heart disease. Chest pain type is coded as
1 = typical angina, 2 = atypical angina, 3 = non-anginal pain, and 4 = asymptomatic.
Of all patients, `r sum(heart$disease == "Yes")`
(`r percent(mean(heart$disease == "Yes"), accuracy = 0.1)`) had angiographic heart
disease. Compared with patients without heart disease, those with heart disease were
more likely to be male and more likely to have asymptomatic chest pain, and
they achieved a lower maximum heart rate.

# Heart Disease Prevalence by Study Site

```{r figure1, fig.cap = "Figure 1. Prevalence of angiographic heart disease at each of the four study sites. Labels above the bars show the prevalence at each site."}
# created by code/03_make_figure1.R
prev_by_site <- readRDS(here::here("output", "prev_by_site.rds"))

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("output", "figure1.png"))
```

Figure 1 shows the proportion of patients with angiographic heart disease at each
study site. Prevalence was lowest in Hungary
(`r percent(prev_by_site$prevalence[prev_by_site$site == "Hungary"], accuracy = 1)`)
and Cleveland
(`r percent(prev_by_site$prevalence[prev_by_site$site == "Cleveland"], accuracy = 1)`),
higher at Long Beach VA
(`r percent(prev_by_site$prevalence[prev_by_site$site == "Long Beach VA"], accuracy = 1)`),
and highest in Switzerland
(`r percent(prev_by_site$prevalence[prev_by_site$site == "Switzerland"], accuracy = 1)`),
where nearly all patients had disease. These differences likely reflect differences
in the patient populations referred for angiography at each site, and they suggest
that study site should be taken into account in later analyses.

# References

Janosi, A., Steinbrunn, W., Pfisterer, M., & Detrano, R. (1989). Heart Disease [Dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C52P4X.
